title: Tamamushi University Magikarp
caption: Hold up. People took actual mail-in exams for a Magikarp card. CoroCoro ran this fake Tamamushi University thing in Japan in 1998, with Pokémon questions and prizes for passing. Imagine studying for a fish. I would have failed and still framed the rejection letter.

title: Masaki Gengar
caption: This Gengar was basically a mail-order evolution. In Japan, you sent in a Haunter plus a Bill’s PC pass from a vending sheet, and the 1998–99 Evolution Communication campaign sent back this Gengar. A trade evolution done through the actual postal service is kinda nuts.

title: Toyota Arcanine card
caption: You could walk into a Toyota dealership and leave with an Arcanine card. That was an honest-to-goodness 1997 Japanese promotion: dealerships handed out a pamphlet with Pokémon cards. I wonder how many parents thought they were just looking at a Corolla.

title: Hungry Snorlax and its food counters
caption: The Snorlax card came with little FOOD counters. Nintendo gave it out with a music CD when people bought an N64 in Japan during the winter of 1997–98. A console purchase came with a soundtrack, a card, and tiny snacks for the card. Sure, why not.

title: Trade Please! mail-in card
caption: This card literally asked you to trade by mail. In Japan’s 1998 Trade Please campaign, you sent in cards and got a special Charizard, Blastoise, or Venusaur along with the Trade Please! card. Pokémon turned the post office into a link cable.

title: Parent and child Kangaskhan trophy
caption: The Kangaskhan trophy wasn’t for one cracked solo player. A parent and kid had to play together and rack up wins at a 1998 Japanese tournament. Kangaskhan carrying its baby on the card is almost unfairly perfect for that origin.

title: Japan Post Cramorant art card
caption: Why does Cramorant look like an old woodblock print? Because Japan Post put this card in a 2021 stamp box alongside actual postage stamps. The artwork riffs on Hiroshige’s geese and moon. This bird somehow got into fine art AND the mail.

title: Yu Nagaba Eevee sketch card
caption: Eevee looks like it was drawn in five relaxed seconds, and I mean that as a compliment. Artist Yu Nagaba drew a whole Eevee family for a 2023 Japanese TCG collaboration. The spare little line drawings came as random promo cards with eligible purchases.

title: JR Stamp Rally 2000 Eevee
caption: Japan gave out an English Eevee card as a train-rally prize. The 2000 JR Pokémon Stamp Rally sent people around collecting station stamps, then handed out cards that look like they wandered over from an American binder. Little me wouldve considered this a perfect vacation.

title: Starter Triple Get Feraligatr
caption: This Feraligatr came from a postcard tucked into a Japanese e-Card starter deck. The 2001–02 Starter Triple Get campaign had people mail the card in for a shot at one of six holo starter evolutions. Buying the deck was only the beginning of the side quest.

title: Battle Strength mail-in promos
caption: They made you mail in BAR CODES from two decks for these. CoroCoro’s Battle Strength campaign picked 1,000 winners and sent each two three-card promo sets. I can already see the kitchen table covered in cut-up boxes and tape.

title: Shiny Pokémon Present campaign
caption: The shiny chase used to involve scissors and a stamp. This 2010 Japanese campaign asked fans to cut barcodes off TCG products, stick them to a postcard, and enter for shiny promo cards. Your pull was basically a mailroom decision.

title: Pokémon Center Osaka store card
caption: A store in Osaka gave out a card to celebrate a store opening in New York. For a few days in January 2002, purchases at Pokémon Center Osaka got this little storefront promo. The Pokémon retail universe was doing cross-city shoutouts.

title: Neo Imakuni? music CD card
caption: There is a dancing Imakuni? card attached to a Pokémon naming-song CD from 2000. Dude was a musician and an official card character, so naturally the soundtrack and the TCG became one very odd object. This is the sort of binder page that needs an explanation every time.

title: JR Stamp Rally Mewtwo by a Magic artist
caption: This Mewtwo was an English-printed card given out at a 2000 train stamp rally in Japan. Christopher Rush, the artist behind iconic Magic art, drew it. A Japanese rail trip rewarded you with an English Pokémon card by a Magic artist. My binder would need footnotes.

title: Pokémon Center Tokyo Game Boy Light
caption: Pokémon Center Tokyo had its own Game Boy Light in 1998. That Japan-only handheld already glowed in the dark, and the store-opening edition got special Pokémon styling. It looks like a device you’d find in an alternate timeline where every shop had a console.

title: Pokémon Nintendo 64 console
caption: The N64 grew Pikachu cheeks and a Poké Ball power button. Nintendo released this big blue-and-yellow console around the 2000 Pokémon Stadium era. It’s not a sticker skin; they changed the shape of the machine. That thing is a whole roommate.

title: Pikachu Yellow Game Boy Printer
caption: There was a bright yellow Pikachu edition of the Game Boy Printer. It launched in Japan alongside Pokémon Yellow in September 1998, so you could print tiny sticker photos from your Game Boy. A pocket-sized receipt machine for your digital adventures.

title: Original Pocket Pikachu pedometer
caption: Before the Pokéwalker and the GS model, there was this 1998 Pocket Pikachu. Your steps earned Watts to play with a tiny Pikachu on your belt. Pokémon had us doing side quests on a pedometer before anyone called it wellness tech.

title: Tiger Pokédex toy
caption: The 1998 Tiger Pokédex was a chunky electronic encyclopedia you could hold like you had Professor Oak’s actual equipment. It cataloged the original 150 and came out during the first Pokémon merch wave. I would have carried this everywhere and known absolutely nothing useful.

title: Gengar tongue nap cushion
caption: Somebody at Bandai said, what if your nap took place inside Gengar’s mouth? This 2021 official cushion has a long roll-out tongue for your body and a Gengar head behind you. I respect how far they took the bit. Also: no way I’d explain this purchase to my family.

title: Metapod sleeping bag
caption: This is a sleeping bag shaped like Metapod so you can zip yourself into a cocoon. Premium Bandai took preorders in 2020 for a 2021 Japan release. The joke is you literally become the least mobile Pokémon while you sleep. Honestly, kinda ideal.

title: Snorlax Yogibo beanbag
caption: Snorlax finally became a chair. Yogibo and Pokémon Center Japan collaborated in 2023 on Snorlax and Ditto beanbags. It makes perfect sense until you realize the most accurate Snorlax merch is something you collapse into and refuse to leave.

title: Ditto Yogibo beanbag
caption: The Ditto version of that 2023 Yogibo collab is just a giant pink blob to sit on. They could have called it a beanbag and walked away, but Ditto makes it feel like the beanbag is choosing to be furniture. Honestly believable.

title: Slowpoke tail udon
caption: Kagawa made pink-and-white udon noodles to look like Slowpoke’s tail. It’s a regional Pokémon collaboration in Japan’s famous udon prefecture, where Slowpoke became a local PR mascot. The noodles are real. The tail is thankfully just a visual.

title: Chansey playground slide
caption: You can take your kid to a Chansey playground in Fukushima. Pokémon and local governments made these Lucky Parks as part of their regional support work. The slide is a Pokémon, the park is public, and childhood has apparently peaked.

title: Geodude playground
caption: Geodude got hired as playground equipment. Iwate has Geodude Parks through Pokémon’s regional partnership, with character-shaped play structures built for actual kids to climb. Rock type finally found its proper career path.

title: Sandshrew playground
caption: Tottori has a whole Sandshrew Park, which makes sense for a prefecture famous for its sand dunes. It came through Pokémon Local Acts and the local government’s public playground projects. Real-life habitat design, except with slides.

title: Oshawott playground
caption: Mie got Oshawott-themed parks with curvy water-inspired slides. Pokémon’s public playground project announced them for 2025, tying the local support Pokémon to a place kids actually use. It’s nice when a mascot stops being a logo and becomes a slide.

title: Lapras sightseeing boat
caption: Miyagi put Lapras on a real sightseeing boat. Lapras is the prefecture’s support Pokémon, and the boat is part of the local tourism tie-in. You cannot actually ride Lapras across the water, but they got weirdly close.

title: Alolan Vulpix Hokkaido bus
caption: Hokkaido picked snowy Alolan Vulpix as a local ambassador, then put it on a bus. The local Pokémon project uses Vulpix and its icy cousin to show off the region’s seasons. A fox-themed bus through snowy Japan feels almost too on the nose, but I love it.

title: Sandshrew Tottori train
caption: Tottori’s sand dunes got them Sandshrew as a local Pokémon partner, and the little guy has ended up on local transportation too. A Pokémon train for a sand-themed prefecture is a pretty solid bit of regional casting.

title: Pokémon Fossil Museum skeleton
caption: A real museum put Pokémon fossils next to real-world prehistoric specimens. The Pokémon Fossil Museum started in Japan and reached Chicago’s Field Museum in 2026. Seeing an Aerodactyl reconstruction under museum lights is an excellent way to confuse your inner eight-year-old.

title: Excavator Pikachu museum plush
caption: Pikachu has a tiny excavator outfit. It was made for the Pokémon Fossil Museum’s 2026 stop at Chicago’s Field Museum, with a keychain version in the museum shop. I know it’s merch, but a museum-specific construction-worker Pikachu has a lot of lore for one plush.

title: Electric-plated Jolteon craft
caption: An artist made a Jolteon using the actual craft of metalwork and electricity. It was in the POKÉMON × KOGEI exhibition, which brought Japanese craft artists into the Pokémon universe. This is what happens when a thunder dog gets a museum budget.

title: Kimono Pikachu craft plush
caption: Pikachu wore a kimono with a traditional Koji-tsunagi pattern as the souvenir for the POKÉMON × KOGEI craft exhibition. It’s a museum tie-in plush, not just a costume swap: the design points back to the textiles and craft work in the show. Very fancy little mouse.

title: Jigglypuff cat cave
caption: They made a Jigglypuff cave for cats. Pokémon Center’s Playful Partners pet line came out in 2026, and this one is a little hideaway for an animal that already sleeps 18 hours a day. Jigglypuff finally found its ideal audience.

title: Snorlax pet bed
caption: A Snorlax bed for a dog or cat feels like Pokémon merchandise becoming self-aware. This came from the official Playful Partners pet collection in 2026. Your pet gets to sleep on the mascot of sleeping. I might be jelous of the pet.

title: Pikachu Le Creuset kettle
caption: Le Creuset made a Pikachu-yellow kettle. Yes, the fancy cookware people. Its Pokémon Collection launched in July 2024 across selected Asian markets. I have no idea if water boiled in a Pikachu kettle tastes better, but I know I would show every guest.

title: Pikachu Le Creuset cast iron pot
caption: Pikachu became a cast-iron pot. Le Creuset’s second Pokémon Collection phase in 2024 put a Pikachu silhouette on this bright yellow cocotte. A heavy-duty kitchen heirloom and a little electric mouse somehow landed in the same cookware aisle.

title: Pokémon Cafe curry plate
caption: There is a permanent Pokémon Café where Pikachu curry is served on an actual plate, not a screen. The first location opened in Tokyo’s Nihonbashi in 2018, followed by Osaka. Choosing your starter even became part of the curry presentation. Lunch with a side of character lore.

title: Pokémon x Fossil watch
caption: Pokémon and Fossil made a whole 2022 watch line, including steel pieces with Kanto starters and Gengar. It’s funny to see a watch that looks like serious grown-up business until a Pokémon peeks out from the dial. I would check the time way too much.

title: Pokémon GO backpack code
caption: Buy a real GORUCK Pokémon backpack and you got a code for a matching backpack in Pokémon GO. That 2025 collaboration sold the physical bag and your avatar’s bag together. The game character and the human have to coordinate, apparently.

title: Pikachu PC desk cushion
caption: Premium Bandai made a Pikachu plush that lives between you and your keyboard as a PC cushion. There’s a separate armrest piece for typing. The official Singapore Pokémon goods listing is from 2020. Pikachu has entered the ergonomics industry.

title: Pokémon Scale World Nessa with gum
caption: Bandai’s Pokémon Scale World figures are sold in a candy-toy tradition where a piece of gum can come with the toy. The Premium Bandai Nessa and Drednaw set was specifically listed “without gum.” That tiny packaging detail is a whole rabbit hole in Japanese toy culture.

title: Rillaboom figure without gum
caption: This big Rillaboom figure was sold by Premium Bandai with the proud label “without gum.” It’s part of the Scale World line, which grew from candy-toy figures into bigger collector pieces. The fact that the absence of gum is a product feature really gets me.

title: Pokémon GO Asakusa Routes
caption: Pokémon made eight official GO Routes through Tokyo’s Asakusa neighborhood. The 2023 project sent players walking between actual local sights as a kind of guided Pokémon tour. Your phone is now a tour guide, and the research assignment is to go outside.

title: Pokémon Town Seoul Ditto takeover
caption: Seoul’s Jamsil area turned into a Ditto-heavy Pokémon Town for a LOTTE collaboration in 2025. This was a whole real-world district event, not just a store window. Imagine going out for groceries and running into an entire neighborhood doing Ditto cosplay.

title: Pokémon x USJ Halloween parade
caption: Universal Studios Japan put Pokémon into its Halloween entertainment, with a parade and live-show energy far beyond a plush display. The partnership grew from the idea of bringing Pokémon into a physical theme park. DJ Gengar is a career move I did not see coming.

title: Pokémon Center Temporary Store truck
caption: Pokémon Center has temporary shops that can pop up in towns across Japan. The company describes them as a way to bring the store to local fans where and when it fits. A Pokémon Center spawning near you for a while is probably dangerous for your wallet.

title: Pokémon Snap Bulbasaur
caption: Some kid took a picture of Bulbasaur in Pokémon Snap and it became an actual card. For the 1999 CoroCoro contest, winners even mailed in their N64 cartridges so Nintendo could check the shots. The Bulbasaur winner got 20 copies. Imagine explaining that your rarest card came from being good at nature photography in a video game.

title: Burger King gold Pikachu
caption: Burger King really put a gold-plated Pikachu inside a Poké Ball and sold it with a meal. Six metal designs came out for the first movie promotion in 1999, for $1.99 with a value meal. I know it's not a playable card. I also know little me would have kept it in the fanciest spot in my room.

title: Pokémon Pikachu 2 GS
caption: This thing paid you in Watts for walking. The Pokémon Pikachu 2 GS clipped to your belt, let you mess around with Pikachu, and could send Mystery Gifts to Gold, Silver, and Crystal. Japan got it in 1999 and the US in 2000. I wouldve been pacing the kitchen to afford virtual presents.

title: KFC Pokémon plush with card
caption: Before the English Base Set was even on shelves, KFC was handing out Pokémon plush with little character cards attached. That was 1998. So yes, somebody's first Pokémon 'card' may have come with fried chicken. The cards were merch tags, not TCG cards, which makes finding one loose today extra confusing.

title: Burger King Power Card toy
caption: Burger King made a card that pops up into a little moving Pokémon toy. The 2000 Kids Meal Power Cards had 24 plastic designs tied to Pokémon 2000. It's a card, a stand, and a desk toy all fighting for control of the same object. I would've needed every single one, obviously.

title: Ancient Mew
caption: Ancient Mew looked like somebody stole it from the movie's ruins and slipped it into a theater giveaway. The odd symbols and gold layout were part of the Pokémon 2000 promotion. For a lot of kids, a movie ticket led to the strangest-looking card they'd ever held. I still remember trying to read the thing.

title: Pikachu Illustrator
caption: This Pikachu card is basically a trophy for drawing Pikachu. CoroCoro gave Illustrator cards to art-contest winners in the late '90s, right down to the little paintbrush symbol. Imagine drawing a Pokémon and the thank-you note is an actual Pokémon card. That's pretty sick.

title: Birthday Pikachu
caption: You could write your own name on this Pikachu card. The Wizards-era Birthday Pikachu promo went through a Pokémon League Create-a-Card activity, so the blank wasn't a printing mistake. It's your birthday, your Pikachu, your handwriting forever. I'd have absolutely ruined mine with a giant marker.

title: Ooyama’s Pikachu
caption: This Pikachu looks like somebody doodled it on a napkin, which is why I love it. Ooyama's Pikachu is an official Japanese vending card drawn by TCG designer Kouichi Ooyama. Pokémon could have cleaned it up. They printed the goofy little drawing instead, and they were right.

title: Imakuni? card
caption: Who's the guy on the card? That's Imakuni?, a real oddball from Japanese Pokémon music and promotions. Yes, the question mark is part of the name. He ended up on official cards dressed like that, and every time I look at one it feels like I missed about six episodes of an inside joke.

title: Japanese vending sheet cards
caption: In Japan you could buy Pokémon cards from a vending machine on peel-off sheets. The late-'90s Expansion Sheets were glossy and had their own weird little card designs. Peeling a card off a sheet instead of opening a pack sounds wrong for about two seconds, then suddenly I want to do it.

title: Poké Card Creator Pack
caption: Kids drew the art and Pokémon actually printed the winning cards. The 2004 Poké Card Creator Pack came out of a contest for young artists and became a real English TCG release. If I made a drawing at that age and it wound up in somebody else's binder, I would never shut up about it.

title: Pokémon Rumble card game
caption: Pokémon Rumble was a WiiWare game, then Pokémon made cards of it, then made a tabletop game you played with those cards and dice. The 2009 box had a fixed set of cards. That's a game based on a game inside another game. I'm a little lost and I kinda love it.

title: Eevee on the Ball
caption: Eevee got a soccer card. The English FA and Pokémon teamed up on a UK futsal campaign in 2020–21, and the On the Ball promos show Pokémon playing. This isn't a custom someone made after watching a match. The football people and the Pokémon people really got together and made Eevee hit the pitch.

title: Art Academy contest card
caption: Imagine drawing in Pokémon Art Academy and finding out your picture is going on an actual card. That's what the 2014–15 contest did for its winners. Most of my game drawings would've stayed safely on the 3DS, but somebody got a real printed keepsake out of it.

title: The Scream Pikachu
caption: Pikachu is doing The Scream and somehow this is an official card. Tokyo's 2018 Edvard Munch exhibition collaboration gave five Pokémon that dramatic face. I picture somebody coming for a quiet afternoon of art and leaving with a tiny yellow mouse having a full existential crisis.

title: Mario Pikachu
caption: Pikachu put on Mario's hat and got his own card. The 2016 Mario Pikachu crossover sold cards and merch through Pokémon Center stores in Japan. Two Nintendo worlds meeting like this should feel obvious, but the little overalls still get me every time.

title: Pretend Magikarp Pikachu
caption: Pikachu is inside a Magikarp costume. The card came in the Pretend Magikarp & Pretend Gyarados Pikachu box for the 2015 opening of Pokémon Center Hiroshima. They could've printed a normal grand-opening card. Instead the mascot showed up dressed as a fish, and I respect that decision.

title: Van Gogh Pikachu
caption: The Van Gogh Museum put Pikachu in a gray felt hat. The 2023 Amsterdam collaboration made this card part of a museum and education project, with a nod to Van Gogh's self-portraits. I would like to say I went for the art. We both know I'd be looking for this card.

title: Peelable Ditto
caption: The card is lying to you. Some cards in the 2022 Pokémon GO TCG set have another Pokémon printed on top, and you can peel that layer off to find Ditto underneath. A real sticker reveal on a real card. I'd have a hard time deciding whether to peel it or leave the disguise intact.

title: e-Reader dot-code card
caption: Those weird little bars on the card's edge were meant to be scanned. Early-2000s Pokémon e-Reader cards worked with a Game Boy Advance accessory for extra info, sounds, and little games. It feels like checking out groceries, except the grocery item is your Pokémon card and the scanner is a Game Boy.

title: JR East Surfing Pikachu
caption: Getting this Surfing Pikachu involved riding trains and collecting 30 station stamps. JR East's 1997 rally gave finishers a booklet with Surfing Pikachu and Mew. That's not a trip to the card shop. That's a whole transit mission for two pieces of cardboard, and I would've gone.

title: ANA Flying Pikachu
caption: Yes, an airline had a Flying Pikachu card. ANA's Pokémon Jet promotion in 1998 tied the promo to actual Pokémon-covered flights. If somebody handed this to me on a plane as a kid, every later flight would feel like a ripoff.

title: 7-Eleven Jirachi
caption: The surprise card in a 7-Eleven promo pack was Jirachi. Japan's 2003 Pokémon Fair lined up with the Jirachi movie, so a convenience-store stop could become a mini card hunt. Go in for a drink, come out wondering if you need to buy three more packs.

title: Tropical Wind at Worlds
caption: This tropical Pokémon scene was a souvenir from Worlds. Tropical Wind appeared in the 2004 World Championships promo program, with event-stamped versions for staff and competitors. Everyone else is there to compete and this card looks ready to order a drink with a tiny umbrella.

title: Ishihara-GX
caption: They made the president of The Pokémon Company into a GX card for his 60th birthday. Ishihara-GX was a private celebration card in 2017. I can't decide what's funnier: that the office birthday gift was official cardboard, or that the boss could be in your binder.

title: Cool Porygon
caption: Cool Porygon sounds like a nickname somebody made up, but it's on a real card. The English promo came with a Pokémon Stadium N64 bundle in 2000. You buy a console and there, among the cables and manuals, is a Porygon insisting it's cool. Fair enough.

title: Game Boy Meowth
caption: The Game Boy Pokémon Trading Card Game came with a real Meowth card. So you bought a video game about collecting cards and found an actual card in the box. Wizards called it Black Star Promo #10. I keep thinking about the person who opened the box just to add that one card to the binder.

title: Pokémon Center New York card
caption: Pokémon Center New York got a card for its opening in 2001. The Rockefeller Center store had an invitation postcard promotion that could get visitors the exclusive card or a book. A trading card celebrating the opening of a place where you could buy trading cards is wonderfully circular.

title: Bandai Carddass
caption: These Bandai Carddass Pokémon cards came out of Japanese vending machines in 1996. They're more like little Pokédex entries than playable TCG cards, with early art that looks wonderfully different now. Imagine pulling one of these before everybody agreed what a Pokémon card should look like.

title: Meiji chocolate cards
caption: Meiji put collectible Pokémon cards in chocolate products in Japan back in the late '90s. So there was a whole candy-aisle card hunt happening beside the regular TCG. I'd tell myself I was collecting history while eating the evidence.

title: Topsun gum card
caption: That blue-backed Topsun card came with gum. The copyright says 1995, which led to years of 'are these the first Pokémon cards?' arguments, even though the gum product's release history points to 1997. A little piece of candy managed to start a collector debate that never seems to end.

title: Pokémon Bread stickers
caption: Pokémon Bread in Japan comes with a surprise Decochar sticker. Daiichi Pan keeps making new series, so breakfast can turn into a sticker chase. I can see myself pretending I needed another loaf because the last one didn't have the Pokémon I wanted.

title: Pokémon curry
caption: Pokémon curry is an actual dinner item in Japan. Marumiya has sold kid-focused Pokémon curry and seasonings, with the familiar characters right on the package. I like to imagine somebody carefully saving the empty box while the rest of the family just wants to eat.

title: Pokémon Oreo Mew
caption: Oreo put Mew on a cookie in 2021. Sixteen Pokémon designs were stamped into the limited-edition sandwich cookies, and suddenly people were checking dessert like a booster pack. You finally find Mew, then have to decide if you're really gonna eat your pull.

title: Pokémon mini console
caption: Nintendo made a tiny console just for Pokémon. The Pokémon mini arrived in 2001 with its own cartridges, rumble, and infrared. It's small enough to look like a keychain, but nope, that's a whole gaming system. I want to put it next to a regular Game Boy just for the size difference.

title: Pokéwalker
caption: HeartGold and SoulSilver gave you a pedometer so your Pokémon could go for a walk while you did. The Pokéwalker counted steps and talked to the DS game by infrared. I used to think of this as a toy; looking back, Nintendo basically assigned me a walking buddy.

title: Hey You, Pikachu! microphone
caption: Nintendo sold a microphone so you could talk to Pikachu through your N64. Hey You, Pikachu! needed its own voice-recognition unit, and getting Pikachu to listen was an adventure in itself. It's the late '90s version of yelling at a smart speaker, only much cuter.

title: Eevee Tamagotchi
caption: Bandai made an Eevee Tamagotchi in Japan in 2019. You looked after Eevee on the little egg device and its evolution depended on your care. That's so obvious and so weirdly perfect that I had to double-check it took this long to exist.

title: Poké Ball Plus with Mew
caption: A new Poké Ball Plus controller came with Mew inside. It launched with the 2018 Let's Go games, let you swing the ball to throw in-game, and offered the mythical Pokémon as a one-time gift. I love the idea of buying a controller and being told there's a tiny creature living in it.

title: Ditto-as-Pikachu plush
caption: This Pikachu plush has the face of someone who is definitely not Pikachu. Pokémon Center's Transform Ditto line started in Japan in 2016 and made plush versions of Ditto badly impersonating other Pokémon. The face looks off because it's supposed to. Ditto is trying its best, man.

title: The Pikabug car
caption: Nintendo drove a Volkswagen Beetle around dressed as Pikachu, ears and tail included. The Pikabug helped bring Pokémon to American streets in the late '90s. Imagine seeing that in traffic before Pokémon was everywhere. I'd assume I was losing my mind for a second.

title: ANA Pokémon Jet
caption: ANA didn't just put Pokémon on a boarding pass. It painted entire planes with them starting in 1998, and the airline has brought the Pokémon Jets back in later years. I'd spend the whole flight trying to figure out which Pokémon was outside my window.

title: POKÉMON with YOU Train
caption: JR East has a real POKÉMON with YOU Train full of Pikachu details. It runs through the Tohoku region and was created to bring some joy to families after the earthquake. I know trains are supposed to get you somewhere. This one feels like the ride itself is the point.

title: Poké Lids
caption: Japan has Pokémon manhole covers you can go find in actual streets. The Pokémon Company donates these Poké Lids to local governments, with designs tied to their areas. Somewhere along the way, looking down at a utility cover became a legitimate Pokémon collecting activity.

title: Slowpoke’s Kagawa job
caption: Slowpoke got a government-adjacent job in Kagawa. The prefecture made it a tourism ambassador in 2018, playing off its famous udon and the Japanese name Yadon. Now the pink sleepy guy turns up in local products and places. Honestly, I want this level of job security.

title: Magikarp cat fishing rod
caption: The official Pokémon Center made a Magikarp fishing-rod toy for your cat. It's from the Playful Partners pet line, so this is real merch meant for an actual animal to attack. Somewhere a cat is doing more damage to Magikarp than Splash ever did.

title: Giant Wailord plush
caption: Pokémon Center made a Wailord plush that's 57 inches long. That's less 'put it on the shelf' and more 'figure out which furniture is moving out.' Wailord's supposed to be huge, so I get the commitment. I just don't know where the whale sleeps.

title: Pokémon vending machine
caption: Japan has Pokémon vending machines in travel spots. Pokémon Stands sell merch and Card Stands handle TCG products, so your airport layover can become a completely unplanned shopping trip. I would miss my boarding call staring at the thing.

title: Blockbuster Pokémon Snap sticker station
caption: In 1999 you could take pictures in Pokémon Snap, bring the N64 cartridge to Blockbuster, and print your shots as stickers. That is a video store acting like a photo lab for imaginary animals. Honestly one of the coolest bits of old Pokémon tech I've ever heard of.

title: Domino’s Snorlax LV.X
caption: Domino’s once handed out a Snorlax LV.X card with pizza in Japan. This was the 2008–09 Exciting Pokémon Pack campaign, which is such a wild place for a serious-looking TCG promo to come from. Imagine opening dinner and finding this guy staring back like he ate your order.

title: Uniqlo Warm Pikachu
caption: This Pikachu card came with kids’ HEATTECH clothing at Uniqlo in Japan in late 2014. His move is literally about getting warm. I kinda love that a thermal shirt came with a Pokémon card that understands the assignment.

title: Lucky Stadium Hokkaido
caption: Some Pokémon cards were basically regional postcards. This Lucky Stadium was a prize for taking part in the 2000 World Challenge in Japan, with art tied to the local area. A tournament card that remembers where you actually played is pretty cool.

title: 2005 Championship Arena
caption: This Japanese Championship Arena card went to people who won a Stage 4 match at Battle Road Autumn 2005. The event had six stages, with a Card Laboratory researcher waiting at the end. They made an actual card for climbing that ladder, which feels like a real-life gym badge.

title: Dark Fearow guidebook card
caption: Dark Fearow was tucked into a strategy guide for the Japan-only Pokémon Card GB2 Game Boy Color game. So the guide for a digital card game came with a physical card. The cardboard loop is complete.

title: McDonald’s Pokémon-e pack
caption: Japan’s 2002 McDonald’s Pokémon-e Minimum Pack gave out actual e-Reader compatible cards. You could get lunch and a little dot-code card to scan with a Game Boy Advance. That meal had peripherals.

title: Southern Islands postcard pack
caption: Southern Islands was sold in Japan as little three-card postcard sets in 1999, tied to the second movie. Put all the art together and it becomes a tropical scene. Somebody made a binder page you could basically vacation in.

title: Tropical Present jumbo postcard
caption: This oversized Tropical Present card was mailed to Japanese Pokémon Fan Club members who built up 100 GET points. It was a postcard you earned by being extremely committed to Pokémon in 1999. Imagine getting this in the actual mail.

title: Kraft Australia Dark Charmeleon
caption: Even Kraft had a Pokémon card oddity. Australia got a special Dark Charmeleon print through a Kraft promotion around 2000. A Team Rocket card crossing paths with grocery packaging is a combination I did not see coming.

title: Rayquaza coaster card
caption: This Rayquaza promo was tied to the Rayquaza coaster at PokéPark, the temporary Pokémon theme park in Nagoya in 2005. A card as a souvenir of a specific ride? I’d be guarding it harder than my seatbelt.

title: PokéPark Edy payment card
caption: PokéPark used its own Pokémon-themed Edy card to pay for rides in Nagoya in 2005. It’s a theme park ticket, a payment gadget, and a little collectible all mashed together. You had to load money just to enter the side quest.

title: PokéPark Poké Ball Ferris wheel
caption: There was a Poké Ball Ferris wheel at the temporary PokéPark in Nagoya in 2005. Whole ride cabins looked like Poké Balls. You could literally sit inside the thing we’ve been throwing at creatures for years.

title: Buzzwole arm pillow
caption: They sold Buzzwole’s big flexing arm as a pillow. It was in Pokémon Center Japan’s 2024 BUG OUT! collection of Bug-type merch. The same creature that looks like a mosquito bodybuilder is now supporting your neck during a nap.

title: Venipede pullback car
caption: Venipede became a little pullback race car in the 2024 BUG OUT! collection. Pokémon Center based it on the bug’s Speed Boost ability, which is a very elaborate justification for making a centipede zoom across your desk. I want one.

title: Life-size Larvesta plush
caption: This Larvesta plush is life-size. Pokémon Center put it in the 2024 BUG OUT! collection, apparently for people whose ideal roommate is a big fuzzy fire larva. It looks softer than its typing suggests.

title: Life-size Porygon plush
caption: Porygon is a blocky computer duck and somebody made a life-size plush of it. Pokémon Center Japan’s 2024 Night Arcade collection went full retro-game weirdness. How do you make polygons cuddly? Apparently like this.

title: Slowpoke tail-linking plush
caption: These Slowpoke plushes connect by their tails. Pokémon Center’s 2024 Slowpoke collection turned that ridiculous evolution lore into a toy you can chain across your couch. There has to be a limit. I do not want to find it.

title: Ditto snack-stealing plate
caption: This little Ditto plate is designed so Ditto looks like it’s reaching for your snacks. Pokémon Center Japan released it in a 2025 Ditto collection. A plate that gives your food a tiny thief is so stupidly charming.

title: Vibrating Sentret and Furret hug plush
caption: Pull Sentret and Furret apart and they buzz back together like a little hug. Pokémon Center Japan added this pair to its 2025 trembling-hug plush line. The pre-evolution even has teary eyes. I was not expecting a battery-free toy to hit me in the feelings.

title: Twisty Rayquaza plush
caption: Rayquaza became a long bendy plush you can wrap and pose. It was part of Pokémon Center Japan’s 2025 collection for noodly Pokémon. Of course the sky dragon ended up functioning like a fuzzy twist tie.

title: Serperior pen stand
caption: Somebody made Serperior coil around your pens. It came from that same 2025 Pokémon Center collection devoted to long, winding Pokémon. My desk would instantly become a tiny throne room for pencils.

title: Pawmo reveal glass
caption: Pawmo only really shows up on this glass when you pour in a drink. Pokémon Center Japan put it in a 2024 Pawmo collection. It’s like a very low-stakes magic trick that also reminds you to hydrate.

title: Pawmo cup-hugging spoon
caption: This spoon hangs off the edge of your cup like Pawmo is clinging on. Pokémon Center released it with the 2024 Pawmo goods. That tiny detail is doing an unreasonable amount of work for my coffee.

title: Gengar gaming headset
caption: Razer made a Gengar headset with big ghost ears. This official collab got a wider release in 2025 after earlier regional availability. It looks like the headset is about to haunt whoever is on the other end of the call.

title: Pokémon Pinball battery cart
caption: Pokémon Pinball came on this weird oversized Game Boy Color cartridge with a AAA battery stuck in it. Nintendo released it in 1999 so the game could rumble in your hands. The cartridge looks like it ate another cartridge.

title: Pokémon Typing keyboard
caption: Nintendo bundled a Bluetooth keyboard with a Pokémon typing game on DS in 2011. You learned to spell by typing Pokémon names while a handheld sat on a stand. It’s like homework disguised as an extremely specific peripheral.

title: Pokémon Battrio puck
caption: Before every collectible had a QR code, there were Pokémon Battrio pucks. The 2007 Japanese arcade game had you place chunky plastic Pokémon tokens on a machine to battle. It’s a binder collection that refused to fit in a binder.

title: Physical Z-Ring toy
caption: They made a physical Z-Ring toy that flashed and vibrated along with Sun and Moon. Released around the 2016 games, it let you act out the over-the-top Z-Move pose in your living room. I would have knocked over a lamp doing it.

title: Pokémon GO Plus + sleep button
caption: The GO Plus + button tracks your sleep and has Pikachu sounds. It launched with Pokémon Sleep in 2023, so this Poké Ball-ish puck wants you to go catch monsters AND go to bed on time. Weirdly supportive little gadget.

title: McDonald’s air-pump Pikachu
caption: McDonald’s put a Pikachu air-pump toy in a 2001 Pokémon promotion. It was one of several little mechanical Pokémon toys, not a card or a normal figure. The Happy Meal era was full of tiny engineering experiments.

title: Welch’s Pokémon jelly glass
caption: Welch’s sold Pokémon jelly in jars meant to become drinking glasses once you finished the jelly. Late-90s American grocery aisles had fully turned into a Pokémon scavenger hunt. Eat the jam, keep the cup. That is a strong deal.

title: Kraft Pokémon macaroni shapes
caption: Kraft made Pokémon-shaped macaroni and cheese around 2000. A food item that asks you to identify your pasta before eating it feels very on brand for that era. I wonder how many Pikachus survived the boil with both ears.

title: Pokémon Wonder twig creature
caption: Pokémon Wonder hid creatures in a real forest made from leaves, twigs, and other natural stuff. It opened at Yomiuriland in 2021 as an outdoor scavenger hunt. You don’t tap a screen; you squint at a pile of branches until it becomes a Pokémon.

title: MIMARU Snorlax hotel room
caption: You can book a Pokémon hotel room with a giant Snorlax waiting on the bed. MIMARU’s Pokémon Rooms spread across its apartment hotels in Japan. The sleep mascot is there to make sure you never leave your room, apparently.

title: Pikachu Outbreak parade
caption: Yokohama turned city streets into a Pikachu invasion starting in 2014. The annual Outbreak events brought crowds of suited-up Pikachus out for parades and dancing. One Pikachu is cute; fifty marching toward you is a whole new emotion.

title: Pokémon Goita board game
caption: Pokémon made a version of goita, a traditional game from Noto, in 2026. The pieces became Pokémon and the collab helped share a local game with new people. I like when a franchise wanders into an old board game and actually learns the rules.

title: Geodude transparent-leg plush
caption: Iwate’s mascot Geodude has a problem: the Pokémon floats, but a person in a costume needs legs. The running gag is transparent legs. That joke even made it into official merch, and I’m still stuck on a rock monster having invisible pants.

title: Wedding Pikachu plush couple
caption: There is an official pair of bride-and-groom Pikachu plushes. Pokémon Center Japan released them with its 2018 Garden Wedding line, because apparently your wedding registry needed electric rodents. Honestly they look happier than most cake toppers.

title: Tiffany Poké Ball jewelry box
caption: A Tiffany gold Pikachu pendant came inside a Tiffany Blue Poké Ball. Daniel Arsham’s Pokémon jewelry collab sold luxury pieces in 2023. It’s a Poké Ball that contains something somehow harder to catch than a legendary.

title: Eevee pullback escape plush
caption: This Eevee plush runs away when you pull it back and let go. It came from Pokémon Center Japan’s 2025 line about escape scenes, riffing on Eevee’s Run Away ability. Finally merch that can leave the room before I decide to buy more merch.

title: Bewear trapping Ditto backpack
caption: This backpack has Bewear holding onto Ditto like it’s refusing to let the blob escape. Pokémon Center’s 2025 escape-themed collection turned a very specific Pokémon gag into something you wear to the grocery store. Its a lot. I mean that warmly.

title: Reversible Geodude evolution plush
caption: Unzip this Geodude plush and flip it inside out to evolve it. Pokémon Center Japan put the transformation toy in its 2025 cave collection. Evolution is usually a flash of light; here it’s a zipper and some manual labor.

title: Onix magnetic clip holder
caption: Onix’s head has a magnet so it can grab your paper clips. This came from the Pokémon Center’s 2025 cave-themed merch. Giant rock snake downgraded to desk assistant, and honestly he seems pretty good at the job.

title: Slowpoke yawn umbrella
caption: They made an umbrella printed with Slowpoke yawning. Pokémon Center released it in Japan’s 2024 rain goods line. Standing under a giant sleepy pink face while it pours rain is kind of a mood.

title: Gold Silver heat-reveal tea cup
caption: Pour hot water into this cup and Raikou, Entei, and Suicune appear. Pokémon Center Japan made it for Gold and Silver’s 25th anniversary in 2024. It’s an encounter animation for your tea. I’d keep boiling water just to see it again.

title: Horsea watering can
caption: Horsea became a watering can. Pokémon Center made it in 2024 for the Pokémon Concierge merch line, based on the stop-motion show’s little resort world. A Water-type that waters your plants may be the most sensible weird thing here.

title: NOUSAKU metal Pikachu casting
caption: A Japanese metal foundry turned Pokémon into cast metal craft objects. The NOUSAKU collab in 2024 even used workshops to show how the pieces are made. Your Pikachu now has the heft of an heirloom instead of a plush.

title: Pokémon card plush stand
caption: Pokémon Center made a plush stand to prop up your actual cards in 2025. Collecting crossed streams with toy collecting: your cardboard gets its own tiny stuffed furniture. That’s kinda adorable and a little ridiculous.

title: Pokémon jewelry wedding ring
caption: You can buy actual Pokémon engagement and wedding rings from Japanese jeweler U-Treasure. These aren’t novelty plastic; it’s fine jewelry built around characters people grew up with. Imagine telling grandma Pikachu helped choose the ring.

title: 1999 talking Pikachu toy
caption: Hasbro’s late-90s electronic Pikachu had light-up cheeks and sounds. Press the buttons quickly and the audio could land in some accidental, uh, grown-up territory. This was a real first-wave toy, and the glitchy charm is very 1999.

title: PiPiPi Adventurer manga phone card
caption: This 1996 Japanese phone card used art from the PiPiPi Adventurer Pokémon manga. Pikachu looks like he knows my long-distance bill is about to be embarrassing.

title: CoroCoro Red phone card
caption: Imagine flexing your trainer credentials at a pay phone. Obsessed. CoroCoro Comics had this Red-themed prepaid telephone card in 1996.

title: CoroCoro Green phone card
caption: The version exclusives followed us all the way to the phone booth, huh. The Green counterpart was another 1996 CoroCoro Comics phone card.

title: Articuno phone card
caption: I would call exactly one person and then frame the bird. This Articuno design appears in a 1996 group of Japanese Pokémon telephone cards.

title: Zapdos phone card
caption: A Zapdos design from the same 1996 Japanese prepaid telephone card series. Electric-type on a phone card is frankly showing off. ⚡

title: Moltres phone card
caption: A fire bird on something you're supposed to slide into a machine. Sure, fine. The Moltres version completed that 1996 legendary-bird phone card trio.

title: Televi-Kun phone card
caption: A magazine freebie that could literally phone your mom? Peak technology. This 1998 telephone card was tied to Japan's Televi-Kun children's magazine.

title: Pokémon Center Tokyo opening phone card
caption: Forget the souvenir mug, I want the tiny functional grand-opening phone rectangle. A 1998 prepaid card commemorated the Pokémon Center Tokyo grand opening.

title: Pokémon Center Osaka phone card
caption: Pokémon Center Osaka received its own commemorative telephone card around its 1998 opening. They made a store-opening collectible you could spend on a call. Brutal choice.

title: Mewtwo Strikes Back phone card
caption: Mewtwo being a pay-phone accessory feels deeply against his entire vibe. This was one of several Japanese prepaid cards for the 1998 first Pokémon movie.

title: The 64 DREAM phone card
caption: Nintendo magazine to telephone booth pipeline. We really lived like this. A 1999 Pokémon telephone card was tied to the Japanese Nintendo magazine The 64 DREAM.

title: Third-anniversary phone card
caption: Third birthday and already in telecommunications. Overachiever. A 1999 Japanese telephone card set celebrated Pokémon third anniversary.

title: Lugia movie phone card
caption: A telephone card promoted the 1999 Japanese Lugia movie. The guardian of the sea is apparently handling my collect call.

title: 1999 ANA airline phone card
caption: A plane, a pay phone, and a Pokémon. My travel anxiety has merch. ANA used Pokémon on a 1999 Japanese telephone card during its airline tie-ins.

title: 2000 ANA airline phone card
caption: Yes I would keep an expired airline phone card like a treasured heirloom. ✈️ ANA followed with a different Pokémon telephone card design in 2000.

title: Famitsu magazine phone card
caption: Game journalism used to come with minutes, apparently. Japanese game magazine Famitsu had a Pokémon phone card around 2000.

title: Shiny Concert Pichu phone card
caption: This 2001 Japanese phone card was labeled Shiny Concert and featured Pichu. Tiny concert attendee, extremely expensive imaginary phone call.

title: Latias and Latios movie phone card
caption: The movie's Venice-ish vibes somehow made it onto a pay phone. Beautifully random. A telephone card was produced for Japan's 2002 Latias and Latios movie.

title: Shining Charizard phone card
caption: A sparkly Charizard you can't put in your deck, only your wallet. Rude. This collector-documented Japanese telephone card features Shining Charizard circa 2002.

title: Pokémon Stadium phone card
caption: A cartridge game on a card for calling people. Technology was a soup. A Japanese telephone card paired Pokémon Stadium-era artwork with Nintendo 64 branding.

title: Pocket Monster Mato Pikachu phone card
caption: This collector-documented Japanese prepaid phone card features a Pikachu from the Pocket Monster Mato artwork; its original issue date is uncertain. Pikachu has a phone card from an obscure comic tie-in and my brain is now a filing cabinet.

title: Kellogg's Battle Tops
caption: My breakfast prize could duel. Cereal was operating at full power. Kellogg's cereal boxes during Gen II packed one of eight spinning Pokémon Battle Tops.

title: PiPiPi Adventurer Pikachu telephone card
caption: The tiny mouse got a manga spin-off AND a way to call home. I love his range. The 1996 Japanese PiPiPi Adventurer manga also had this separate Pikachu prepaid telephone card.

title: Pokémon Eggo waffles
caption: They put Gengar on breakfast and then tried to upsell syrup infrastructure. Respect. Kellogg's made Pokémon-outline Eggo waffles in August 2000 and offered a mail-in Pikachu syrup holder.

title: Osaka Pokémon Center phone-card set
caption: A collector documents this telephone-card set commemorating the Pokémon Center Osaka opening in 1998. Opening a store and issuing functional phone minutes as merch? That is a flex.

title: Wild Cherry Pokémon Pop-Tarts
caption: Pikachu frosting sounds like a crime and I would've eaten twelve. The Pokémon 2000 movie tie-in pastry had yellow Pikachu frosting and Pokémon-shaped sprinkles.

title: Poké Berry Pop-Tarts
caption: Blue breakfast AND a toy, the exact marketing pitch to defeat ten-year-old me. A later Pop-Tarts movie tie-in had blue frosting, Poké Ball sprinkles and a metallic figure in the box.

title: Kellogg's marshmallow Pokémon cereal
caption: I would spend nine minutes separating marshmallow Pikachu from the cereal. Kellogg's released oat rings with Pokémon-shaped marshmallows in 2000.

title: Kellogg's Canadian Game Tip cards
caption: Canadian Kellogg's boxes in 1999 contained three random game-tip cards from a 20-card set. Cereal taught you Pokémon Snap and handed you homework in card form.

title: Mewtwo movie phone card, second design
caption: Mewtwo would absolutely refuse my call and yet I need the card. This is a second collector-documented prepaid phone card tied to the 1998 Mewtwo Strikes Back movie in Japan.

title: Mewtwo movie phone card, third design
caption: A movie promo you can actually spend talking about the movie. Very efficient. The 1998 movie had multiple Japanese phone-card designs; this one uses a different illustration from the first two.

title: Lugia movie phone card, second design
caption: Sea guardian as phone credit is such a funny little downgrade. 🌊 This is another Japanese prepaid card for the 1999 Lugia movie.

title: Lugia movie phone card, third design
caption: The collector archive records this third telephone-card design from the 1999 Lugia movie campaign. Somewhere there was a whole Lugia phone plan and I missed it.

title: Poké Gum stamped pieces
caption: They put the collectible ON the chewable thing. Collector nightmare. Toymax's Candy Planet Poké Gum had Pokémon stamped onto the gum and a puzzle card on the backing.

title: Tsurisage gum and stickers
caption: Every layer of this gum was collectable. I'd never reach the gum. Japanese Tsurisage sold eight-piece gum strips with Pokémon wrappers, stamped gum and a sticker per piece.

title: ANA airline Pokémon phone card, extra design
caption: The airline wanted Pikachu on your plane AND in your phone booth. Unreasonably persuasive. ANA issued multiple Pokémon-themed prepaid telephone cards alongside its airline promotions in Japan; this is a separate collector-documented design.

title: 2010 Minccino marshmallow tin
caption: Pokémon Center Japan's November 2010 collector tin held ten marshmallows and a figure on the lid. Minccino guarding marshmallows has very polite bouncer energy.

title: Pichu and Pikachu short-film phone card
caption: Two tiny chaos agents handling my outgoing calls. Yeah, okay. The Pichu and Pikachu short film got its own Japanese prepaid telephone card around the 2000 movie season.

title: Celebi movie phone card
caption: Time travel on a card for making calls from a fixed location. Deliciously backwards. This Japanese telephone card promoted the 2001 Celebi: a Timeless Encounter movie.

title: Jirachi movie telephone card
caption: A wishing star on phone credit. My wish is that someone picks up. A Japanese prepaid telephone card promoted the 2003 Jirachi movie.

title: BANPRESTO Pikachu telephone card
caption: Banpresto put Pikachu on a Japanese prepaid telephone card, documented in a collector archive. A company promo that is also money for the pay phone. Sneaky useful.

title: Topps gum-filled lollipop
caption: Lollipop, gum, sticker. A three-act play for my teeth. Topps sold Pokémon lollipops around 2000 with Bazooka gum inside and one of 39 stickers.

title: TOMY Lugia telephone card
caption: Lugia had toy-company phone minutes too. This bird was booked and busy. TOMY produced this Lugia-branded Japanese telephone card; the precise issue date is not documented in the collector archive.

title: Bartons Pikachu marshmallow buddies
caption: Twelve squishy Pikachus staring at me from a box. I need a minute. Bartons Candy packed a dozen Pikachu-shaped marshmallows together.

title: SHOWA NOTE Pikachu and Togepi card
caption: Stationery maker Showa Note issued a Japanese phone card featuring Pikachu and Togepi; its exact date is not confirmed. A stationery company made a calling card. The office supplies got ambitious.

title: Pineapple chew battle wrappers
caption: The candy wrapper can fight. Please let me hoard my trash in peace. Pineapple candy strips came in wrappers that doubled as 50 collectible rock-paper-scissors battle cards.

title: Dragonite and Pikachu telephone card
caption: Dragonite looks ready to deliver the message by hand anyway. 📬 A collector documents this Japanese prepaid phone card pairing Dragonite and Pikachu; the original issuer and date are unclear.

title: Darkrai movie popcorn bucket
caption: Refills AND a charm? I would have dragged that bucket through the whole theater. Japanese screenings of The Rise of Darkrai had a Poké Ball popcorn bucket with a detachable Pikachu charm and refills.

title: Seven o’clock Pikachu phone card
caption: This Pikachu telephone card appears in a Japanese collector archive; its issuer and issue date remain unclear. Seven o’clock Pikachu sounds like a very polite alarm I would snooze.

title: Betty Crocker Pokémon Rolls
caption: Punch Red sounds like a move I use against my dentist. General Mills released Punch Red Pokémon fruit candy rolls under Betty Crocker in 1999.

title: Pokémon Twist Pops
caption: Snorlax on a candy cap knows I'm opening a second one. The 1999 fruit candy sticks had twisting tops shaped like Bulbasaur, Pikachu, Psyduck or Snorlax.

title: Nestlé Pokémon Wonder Ball
caption: A chocolate egg with a second tiny mystery inside. My impulse control was cooked. A 2001 Wonder Ball had Pokémon candy and a sticker tucked inside a chocolate shell.

title: Pocket Monster Shogakukan phone card
caption: The Japanese publisher Shogakukan appears on this Pokémon prepaid phone card documented by collectors. Publishing, Pokémon, payphones. The 90s business plan was just all the P words.

title: Heinz Pokémon pasta can
caption: Version-exclusive canned pasta. What a time to be alive. Heinz sold Pokémon-shaped pasta in tomato sauce around 2000, initially in Red and Blue versions.

title: Oscar Mayer Lunchables cutout cards
caption: My collectible card came pre-attached to lunch meat packaging. Iconic chaos. US Lunchables boxes in 1999 had 36 collectible Pokémon game-tip cards printed on the cardboard for kids to cut out.

title: Pokémon nonalcoholic Shan Meri
caption: Piplup in a festive bottle pretending to be champagne. Honestly me at parties. Japanese Pokémon Diamond & Pearl Shan Meri was a grape-flavored holiday sparkling drink in character wrapping.

title: Tonbo Pokémon Ramune bottle
caption: Tonbo sold Pokémon-branded ramune soda in Japan in a 200 mL glass bottle; this photo shows a later character design. A fizzy Pikachu bottle with that little marble stopper? Hydration suddenly has a minigame.

title: Italian Valfrutta bottle caps
caption: Two hundred forty-nine bottle caps. My kitchen would become a museum. Italian Valfrutta fruit juice bottles carried 249 collectible Pokémon caps in 2000–01.

title: Polish Kubuś Pokémon juice boxes
caption: Bulbasaur juice-box diplomacy crossed borders. I love this. Polish Kubuś sold 200 mL juice boxes with Pikachu and the Kanto starters.

title: TOMY Ash telephone card
caption: Ash has a phone card? That boy was never home to answer it. TOMY also produced a Japanese Pokémon telephone card featuring Ash; the collector archive does not pin down its year.

title: Japan Post 84-yen TCG stamp sheet
caption: Card art finally got a second job delivering my electric bill. The companion July 2021 84-yen sheet used Pokémon TCG illustrations as legitimate postage.

title: Japan Post Pokémon stamp box
caption: They put the post office in a Poké Ball and somehow it worked. Japan Post sold its 2021 Pokémon Stamp Box in a Pokémon-themed collector box with stamps and TCG pieces.

title: Japan Post Beauty Looking Back Pikachu
caption: Pikachu doing art history is a museum date I would actually attend. The 2021 Stamp Box included a Pikachu TCG promo riffing on a famous Japanese postage stamp design.

title: Japan Post stamp-box die-cut cards
caption: The 2021 Pokémon Stamp Box held three die-cut cards alongside actual postage and TCG promos. An envelope of stamps, a card game, and extra cardboard. Mail had a loot table.

title: Slowpoke Kagawa postbox
caption: The most leisurely postal employee is also the building. Iconic. A functional Slowpoke postbox debuted in Takamatsu, Kagawa, in March 2021 as part of Pokémon Local Acts.

title: Slowpoke mail truck
caption: My package is late, but if Slowpoke is driving I forgive everything. The Kagawa Slowpoke postal project in 2021 also decorated a working mail truck.

title: Yokohama Eevee postbox
caption: Eevee can evolve into eight things and chose municipal infrastructure. Japan Post installed this real Eevee postbox at Yokohama City Hall in July 2021.

title: Yokohama Piplup postbox
caption: A real Piplup postbox appeared at Yokohama Sakuragi Post Office for the 2021 stamp launch. Piplup waiting politely for postcards is almost too much for me.

title: France La Poste Pokémon stamp sheet
caption: Pikachu international postal career is thriving, mine is mostly spam. La Poste released licensed Pokémon postage in France in 2024; this is a sheet of its character stamps.

title: Pokémon Tretta arcade square
caption: We had actual little plastic Pokémon tiles to feed an arcade machine. Incredible. Takara Tomy A.R.T.S. and Marvelous launched Pokémon Tretta in Japanese arcades in 2012 with collectible square pieces.

title: Pikaqu bootleg talking Pikachu
caption: Pikaqu is what happens when Pikachu gets a fake ID and a voice box. I adore his audacity. Pokémon collector Aspenth showed this unauthorized “Pikaqu” talking figure in a 2025 Johto Times interview. It riffs on the 1998 TOMY talking Pikachu toy; its maker and production date are unknown.

title: Tretta Pikachu arcade square
caption: Pokémon Tretta machines in Japan dispensed collectible square Pokémon pieces; this Pikachu one was scanned to play. Pikachu became a chunky little arcade tile and I need a pocketful.

title: Pokémon Ga-Olé disk
caption: Cards were apparently too flat. Time for arcade Pokémon rectangles. Pokémon Ga-Olé followed Tretta in Japan in 2016, dispensing long collectible plastic disks from an arcade cabinet.

title: Pokémon Mezastar tag
caption: This thing looks like a hotel key for Pikachu private club. Pokémon Mezastar debuted in Japan in 2020 and dispensed chunky Pokémon tags for its arcade battles.

title: Mezastar Memory tag
caption: Even the machine memory came as a lil physical artifact. I get it. The Mezastar Memory tag tracked progress in the arcade system separately from collectible Pokémon tags.

title: Mezastar Charizard tag
caption: Pokémon Mezastar arcade machines dispensed collectible Pokémon tags, including this Charizard design. A tiny plastic Charizard with the energy of a VIP pass. 🔥

title: Pokémon Get Round and Round machine
caption: It looks like a tiny carnival booth dedicated to taking my coins. Namco Bandai released this Japanese Pokémon medal arcade game in April 2010 in yellow and blue cabinets.

title: Pokémon Card Game Gacha arcade
caption: The pack-opening dopamine got its own cabinet. Extremely dangerous for me. A Japanese Pokémon Card Game Gacha machine dispensed cards through an arcade game format.

title: Space World 1997 Mew event flyer
caption: You physically handed a machine your cartridge to meet one mythical little guy. This flyer advertised the 1997 Space World Mew distribution, where cartridges were loaded using a dedicated machine.

title: Space World Celebi machine
caption: Nintendo Space World 2000 used a dedicated machine to distribute Celebi to Gold and Silver cartridges. A shrine to plugging in a Game Boy so the onion fairy could move in.

title: Pokémon Center New York distribution station
caption: A retail kiosk for downloading a creature into your pocket. Magic, honestly. The New York store used a Gotta Catch ’Em All Station to distribute rare Pokémon to game cartridges in the early 2000s.

title: Wishing Star Jirachi distribution result
caption: You went to an event to have a wish delivered through a cable. 🥹 A 2003 event distributed Wishing Star Jirachi to compatible Game Boy Advance games; this photo shows Jirachi in the game after transfer.

title: Tiger Electronic Pokémon yo-yo
caption: A yo-yo that also needs batteries. This is what the 90s were for. Tiger Electronics made light-up, noise-making Pokémon electronic yo-yos in 1999.

title: Hasbro touch-activated Pokémon figure
caption: Hasbro made electronic Pokémon figures from 1998 to 2000 that reacted when you touched two contacts on the base. A tiny Pokémon demands human conductivity before it will speak. Fair.

title: Zanzoon Pokémon Trainer Mission
caption: A whole tiny training quest sealed in one plastic gadget. No Wi-Fi, just vibes. Zanzoon made a self-contained electronic Pokémon Trainer Mission toy with a digital collection.

title: Pokémon Tazos snack discs
caption: The chip bag held a little battle coin. My lunch money was doomed. Pokémon Tazos were collectible printed discs distributed with Frito-Lay snacks in Mexico around 2000.

title: Penny Eevee backpack
caption: The game character backpack escaped into real life and is cuter than my whole closet. Pokémon Center released a wearable version of Penny’s Eevee backpack in 2025, modeled on Scarlet and Violet.

title: JimmyPaul Pokémon runway coat
caption: Designer JimmyPaul debuted a Pokémon runway collection in February 2026 with Difuzed pieces for Pokémon Center. The Pokémon are serving fashion week and I am serving laundry chair.

title: Pokémon x CDG shirt
caption: A Pikachu outfit for people whose closet has an actual point of view. Pokémon and Comme des Garçons released a fashion collaboration in 2022.

title: Pokémon x Skinnydip phone case
caption: My phone could be in a Pokémon case and suddenly my cracked screen is styling. Pokémon and Skinnydip London brought a 2024 collection of bright accessories to Pokémon Center.

title: 100 Thieves Pokémon jersey
caption: Esports jersey but make it childhood creature obsession. Sure, I’m in. A 2025 Pokémon and 100 Thieves clothing drop included competitive-gaming-inspired looks.

title: Pokémon Concierge Furret wood carving
caption: Pokémon Center recreated the wooden Furret ornament from Haru’s room in Pokémon Concierge as a figure in 2025. They made set dressing from a stop-motion show into merch. Furret has an agent.

title: Pokémon Concierge Spheal paperweight
caption: Spheal new job is sitting on my unpaid paperwork and looking round. The 2025 Pokémon Concierge goods line included a Spheal-inspired paperweight.

title: Pokémon Concierge Alolan Exeggutor shirt
caption: Three heads, one vacation shirt, zero ability to act normal at brunch. Pokémon Center Japan’s 2025 Concierge collection included a tropical Alolan Exeggutor aloha shirt.

title: Dratini handle mug
caption: The mug has a lil dragon for a handle. I’d apologize every time I grabbed it. A 2025 Pokémon Center Japan collection made a mug with Dratini as the handle.

title: Gyarados waterfall shirt
caption: The 2025 slithery-Pokémon line printed a Gyarados doing Waterfall on a T-shirt. A wearable dramatic fish incident. Obviously I need it.

title: Seviper wraparound shirt
caption: The snake is literally trying to style me. Let her. 🐍 The same 2025 Japanese Pokémon Center line used Seviper coiling pose on a shirt.

title: Transparent Dragapult figure
caption: The stealth dragon is now a see-through display object. Beautiful contradiction. Pokémon Center Japan’s 2025 invisible-Pokémon collection included a clear Dragapult figure.

title: Transparent Mew figure
caption: Mew is trying to disappear but remains the cutest thing on my shelf. That same 2025 Pokémon Center collection turned Mew into a clear figure to evoke invisibility.

title: Hama-chan’s Slowking
caption: A comedian got his own Slowking card?? Hama-chan’s Slowking was tucked into the September 1999 CoroCoro Comic in Japan, tied to Masatoshi Hamada’s voice role in the second Pokémon movie. It’s a movie cameo, a celebrity card, and a very confused king all at once. 👑

title: Team Rocket’s Meowth CD card
caption: Meowth’s Party was an actual music CD single in 1999, and it came with this Team Rocket’s Meowth card. I know Pokémon made songs, but a physical card riding along with Meowth’s recording career is kind of incredible. 🎤

title: Misty’s Treatment CD card
caption: Misty had a music CD called Riding on Lapras in Japan, and this card came with the single in August 1999. Imagine buying a song and getting Misty as the bonus track in cardboard form. This franchise had no brakes.

title: Duelist magazine Wizards Pikachu
caption: This little Jungle Pikachu got a Wizards stamp and was put in The Duelist magazine in September 1999. That was a magazine for Magic players. Pokémon basically wandered into the neighboring card game’s living room and sat down. 👀

title: Australian PokéTour Pikachu
caption: Australia’s 1999 PokéTour handed out a specially stamped Base Set Pikachu. I love event stamps because they make a totally familiar card say “I was THERE.” A tiny cardboard souvenir of a Pokémon roadshow.

title: Shining Imakuni? membership gift
caption: You joined the Japanese Pokémon Card Fan Club in 2002 and got a Shining Imakuni? card in a zippered holder. The goofy musician somehow got a “Shining” card before a lot of actual Pokémon. I am both delighted and offended on their behalf. ✨

title: Lugia inside Pokémon Card GB2
caption: A physical Lugia card came in the box for Pokémon Card GB2, the Japan-only Game Boy Color sequel from 2001. A card game videogame that packed actual cards is perfectly circular collector logic. Open game, receive game piece.

title: Kecleon movie theater card
caption: If you went to the fourth Pokémon movie in Japan in 2001, you could come home with this Kecleon card. It was a theater giveaway for Celebi: a Timeless Encounter. Kecleon being a little souvenir of a time-travel movie feels strangely right.

title: Pichu Bros. advance ticket card
caption: The Pichu Bros. card was a bonus for buying an advance ticket to the 2002 Latias and Latios movie in Japan. That is an extremely cute way to make me buy a ticket before I even know what day I’m free. ⚡

title: Dark Venusaur magazine card
caption: Dark Venusaur came in volume 10 of Japan’s Pokémon Card Trainers magazine in 2001. It looks like a Team Rocket card that escaped the set and became a magazine insert. I would have bought the issue for the plant alone.

title: Rocket’s Scizor magazine insert
caption: Rocket’s Scizor was an insert in the July 2001 Pokémon Card Trainers magazine. It has the energy of somebody slipping a villain into the mail along with your reading material. Would absolutely have kept the whole magazine.

title: Pikachu fan club Game Boy strap
caption: Joining the Japanese Pokémon Card Fan Club used to get you a membership card AND a little Game Boy strap in the mail. The club started in 1999 through Trainers magazine. I’d probably still have the strap on my keys 27 years later.

title: Meiji chocolate TCG promo 2004
caption: In 2004, Meiji chocolate boxes in Japan held an actual TCG promo in a little silver-striped sleeve. Not a sticker, a playable card. I would have been “buying chocolate for the card” with a suspiciously full candy drawer. 🍫

title: Exeggutor Tropical magazine card
caption: This goofy Exeggutor was a glossy magazine version of a card associated with the 1999 Tropical Mega Battle in Hawaii. Pokémon Card Trainers vol. 3 put it in readers’ hands in Japan. Vacation energy delivered through the mail. 🌴

title: Pelipper candy catcher
caption: Pelipper’s mouth became a candy dish. Pokémon Center’s 2025 OTENKI TEAM line turned weather-themed Pokémon into little home objects, and this one will hold your sweets like it caught them at sea. I’d trust this bird with my jellybeans.

title: Tyranitar sand hourglass
caption: A Tyranitar and Gible hourglass filled with sand is kind of perfect. It was part of the 2025 weather-themed OTENKI TEAM collection in Japan. Your timer is a miniature sandstorm with two tiny accomplices. ⏳

title: Clodsire umbrella stand
caption: Paldean Wooper and Clodsire became a diatomaceous-earth umbrella stand in Pokémon Center Japan’s 2024 rain line. They’re Ground/Poison creatures whose job is now drying your umbrella puddle. That’s actual useful weirdness.

title: Wiglett umbrella handle cover
caption: Wiglett pokes out of the handle of your umbrella with this little cover. Pokémon Center released it in its 2024 rain goods. Holding a suspicious beach worm while walking through a rainstorm sounds like an excellent conversation starter. ☔

title: Vaporeon ice cube mold
caption: They made a Vaporeon-shaped ice mold for Pokémon Center’s 2025 “invisible” themed goods. Put water in, freeze it, and the Water Pokémon literally becomes water Pokémon. This might be the most committed bit in my freezer. 🧊

title: Duskull reveal notebook
caption: Pull a sheet out of this notebook cover and Duskull appears. It was in Pokémon Center’s 2025 collection about Pokémon that can turn invisible. A ghost hiding in stationery is so unnecessary and so good.

title: Latias light-projection charm
caption: This mirror charm projects a Latias pattern onto the wall when you shine a strong light at it. Pokémon Center made it for a 2025 invisible-themed collection. It’s basically a tiny secret Pokémon signal, and yes I’d be testing it in every room. ✨

title: Pikachu curry blanket plush
caption: This plush Pikachu is shaped like the rice on a café plate, and the curry is a tiny blanket you tuck over it. Pokémon Center’s 2025 Pokémon Café line made lunch into bedtime. I can’t decide if I want to eat it or put it down for a nap.

title: Eevee frappé pencil case
caption: Eevee became a frappé-shaped pencil case in the Pokémon Café merch line in 2025. I was already susceptible to cute stationery, but now my pens are apparently a blended drink. 🧋

title: Mimikyu “as-is” plush
caption: Pokémon Center made a “just as it is” Mimikyu plush in 2025 that tries to reproduce the weird droopy disguise more faithfully. The whole creature is already a homemade Pikachu costume, so a realistic plush is an oddly layered concept.

title: Poké Ball plush carrier
caption: This Poké Ball shaped pouch is sized to carry your tiny Pokémon fit plush around. It came from Pokémon Center Japan’s 2025 “life with plush” line. We’ve made a carry case for the toy that lives in a fictional carry case. Full circle.

title: Lillie’s tiny plush duffel
caption: Pokémon Center made a mini bag based on Lillie’s big duffel from Sun and Moon in 2025, as part of a collection about living with your plush Pokémon. It’s a deep cut from 2016 that you can actually carry. I respect this level of commitment.

title: Pokémon fit tiny held items
caption: They made tiny Leftovers for your Pokémon fit plush in 2025. Yes, the held item from the games is now an actual little apple-core accessory for a stuffed animal. My plush apparently needed an inventory system. 🎒

title: Voltorb shake pouch
caption: Night Arcade had a pouch with Pokémon pieces inside that shake around when you move it. Pokémon Center’s 2024 line imagined the creatures hanging out in a nighttime game corner. I’m very into a pencil bag that acts like a tiny arcade machine.

title: Old Game Corner poster recreation
caption: Pokémon Center recreated an in-game Game Corner poster as a real poster-and-sticker set for its 2024 Night Arcade line. A background prop from a fictional casino made it onto an actual wall. I want to know who spotted it first. 👀

title: Scream Tail key hook
caption: Scream Tail became a magnetic key hook figure in the 2024 STRANGE PARADOX collection. This prehistoric-looking Jigglypuff relative now holds your house keys. Imagine explaining that evolutionary timeline to somebody at the door.

title: Kingambit pen stand
caption: Kingambit became a pen stand in Pokémon Center’s 2024 comic-book-inspired SECRET of MIGHT line. A boss Pokémon presiding over my desk full of uncapped markers feels appropriately judgmental.

title: Boltund chase measuring tape
caption: This measuring tape acts out Boltund chasing Thievul. It came from that 2024 SECRET of MIGHT collection, where the character gag was built right into the object. Somebody made a tape measure with a plot. I love it.

title: Peeking desk companion plush
caption: These plush Pokémon pop up to watch over your work or studying. Pokémon Center released the “peek out and look” line in late 2024. Being supervised by a tiny creature is either motivational or deeply distracting. Probably both. 👀

title: Human-form Ditto plush
caption: A Ditto plush disguised as a human. Pokémon Center released this purple little oddball in 2026 for Pokopia, where Ditto takes a human shape. The face says “I am doing my best at being a person,” and honestly same.

title: Pikapika Mart shopping Pikachu
caption: Pokémon Center made a pretend Pokémon supermarket in 2025 called Pikapika Mart, complete with a Pikachu plush eco bag that looks ready to shop. A fictional grocery store within a fictional monster world has me considering its opening hours. 🛒

title: Golem rice ball pouch
caption: This onigiri pouch looks like Graveler eating a mossy rock. It was in Pokémon Center’s 2026 “munching” collection. They turned a rock eater into a carrying case for my lunch and now I’m weirdly hungry.

title: Reversible Drowzee dream cushion
caption: Flip this cushion to show Drowzee eating bad dreams. Pokémon Center’s 2026 munching collection took the Pokédex lore and made it a pillow. I think this is supposed to help me sleep but it raises several questions. 😴

title: Zweilous fighting-head plush
caption: A Zweilous plush with movable necks so its two heads can fight over one piece of food. That was an actual design in Pokémon Center’s 2026 munching collection. You have to appreciate merch that includes family drama as a feature.

title: Pincurchin tissue dispenser
caption: You pull tissues right out of Pincurchin’s mouth. Pokémon Center put this in its 2026 munching collection, and I’m sorry but that is the strangest possible way to handle a runny nose. 🤧

title: Spheal clapping wind-up toy
caption: Wind up this Spheal and it claps for its food. Pokémon Center made it for the 2026 munching collection. My lunch has never received that level of encouragement from anyone, including me.

title: Magnetic Zorua twins
caption: Regular Zorua and Hisuian Zorua stick together with magnets in this 2025 Pokémon Center pair. A tiny toy reunion between lookalikes separated by region and centuries. A little too cute for my emotional stability. 🥲

title: Hisuian Zorua sculpted mug
caption: Hisuian Zorua is sculpted right onto this mug. Pokémon Center Japan released matching Zorua and Hisuian Zorua mugs in its 2025 “similar friends” collection. Coffee and cross-generational fox lore before 9 a.m.

title: Pokémon Café Poltchageist matcha
caption: They built a whole Café Poltchageist concept around a Pokémon that is literally haunted matcha. The 2024 Pokémon Center collaboration put the tea ghost in actual cups and goods. This is either brilliant branding or the drink is looking back at you. 🍵

title: Kyoto Pokémon wagashi
caption: A Kyoto confectioner founded in 1865 made seasonal Pokémon wagashi in 2024. These are little traditional sweets, not gummy Pikachus from a convenience store. I would stare at them for ten minutes and then feel bad eating the face.

title: Toyota life-size Miraidon
caption: Toyota engineers built a roughly four-meter life-size Miraidon that can move. It debuted in Toyota City in 2023, translating the motorcycle Pokémon into an actual machine. The kid part of my brain is screaming; the adult part is asking about insurance. 🏍️

title: Paldea at Shima Spain Village
caption: In 2024 a Spanish-themed park in Japan turned part of itself into Paldea, complete with Miraidon and Koraidon food. Pokémon Scarlet and Violet borrowed a lot from Spain, so this crossover feels like the map escaped the Switch.

title: Pokémon Frienda arcade tag
caption: Pokémon Frienda debuted in Japanese arcades in 2024 and spits out chunky physical tags to use in battle. It’s Pokémon collecting in a shape that a binder absolutely cannot help you with. My pockets would be rattling the whole way home.

title: Bruxish and Toxapex toothpaste kit
caption: They made a fake Pokémon-world toothpaste package with Bruxish and Toxapex, and inside is a real toothbrush pouch set. Pokémon Center put it in the 2025 Pikapika Mart supermarket line. Dental care has somehow become worldbuilding. 🪥

title: Bagon dream-of-flight plush
caption: Bagon’s whole thing is dreaming of flight. Pokémon Center’s 2026 flying-themed line made a looped plush you can hang up, so the little dragon finally gets airborne. Okay, thats actually sweet. 🥹

title: Japan Post 63-yen Pokémon stamp sheet
caption: Japan Post issued real 63-yen Pokémon greeting stamps in July 2021, using scenes from the games. Imagine mailing a letter and the stamp has more side quests than your weekend. I would write letters just to use one. 💌
